01Engineering philosophy

How I build AI systems

Calling an LLM API is only a small part of production AI. The rest is engineering: getting the right context to the model, only to people allowed to see it, inside a latency and cost budget, with every step measured, testable and recoverable when it fails.

  1. DISCOVERusers, data, risk
  2. DESIGNarchitecture, contracts
  3. PROTOTYPEthin vertical slice
  4. EVALUATEgolden sets, metrics
  5. SECUREauthz, guardrails
  6. DEPLOYCI/CD, infra as code
  7. OBSERVEtraces, quality, cost
  8. OPTIMIZElatency, tokens
  9. SCALEtenants, load, teams

Production AI is a systems problem

A demo shows that the model can answer. A production system has to show that it answers correctly and safely, repeatedly, for the right user, at a known cost, and that the team will notice when that stops being true. I treat the model as one component behind clear contracts, and I make the rest of the system observable and testable.

RAG Explorer

Ask a question about a small synthetic document set for a fictional company, NovaGrid Corp. The explorer runs each retrieval stage in your browser: query processing, a hashed embedding, hybrid BM25 + vector scoring, reranking, a token-budgeted context builder and an extractive, cited answer.

Retrieval pipeline Local simulation · synthetic documents corpus: —

  3. Embedding
  4. Hybrid retrieval

  6. Reranking

Simulation notes: the "embedding" is a deterministic 256-dimension feature hash of word and character n-grams, standing in for a neural embedding model. The "LLM" step is extractive: it composes the answer only from retrieved sentences, so it cannot add facts that aren't in the corpus. NovaGrid Corp and all its documents are fictional.

05System design

Case study: Enterprise Knowledge Copilot

How I would answer this as a system-design interview question. Enterprise users need answers whose sources are spread across SharePoint, Confluence, Jira and GitHub. Each source has its own permission model, freshness and format.

  1. 1Clarify
  2. 2Constraints
  3. 3High-level design
  4. 4Deep dives
  5. 5Failure modes
  6. 6Evolution
1 · Clarify: functional requirements
  • Natural-language Q&A across four knowledge systems
  • Every claim cites a source the user can open
  • Users only ever see content they are already allowed to read
  • Follow-up questions in a conversation; actions (e.g. create a Jira ticket) need explicit confirmation
2 · Constraints: non-functional requirements
  • Permission correctness is a hard requirement. Quality is tuned within it.
  • Streaming first token fast; a full answer within an agreed p95 budget
  • Predictable cost per request with per-tenant budgets
  • Auditable: who asked what, what was retrieved, what was answered
  • Index freshness measured in minutes for Jira/GitHub, hours acceptable for wikis
3 · High-level design (click a component)
  1. User web, Teams, IDE
  2. SSO via the corporate IdP. The client receives a short-lived access token. The copilot never sees user passwords and never stores long-lived tokens.
  3. Validates the JWT signature, audience and expiry, applies per-user and per-tenant rate limits, sets request IDs for tracing, and enforces payload size limits before any token is spent.
  4. Classifies intent and plans the route (retrieve, call tools, or both), with bounded iterations, per-step timeouts and checkpointed state. Write actions are interrupted for human confirmation.
  5. Resolves the user's groups once per session and turns them into a metadata filter that is pushed down into retrieval. Document ACLs are synced at ingestion time. Results are filtered before ranking, never after generation.
  6. Lexical search catches IDs, ticket keys and error codes. Dense search catches paraphrases. Scores are fused with reciprocal rank fusion, and the system over-fetches to give the reranker candidates.
  7. Rescores the top ~50 candidates against the query. Deduplicates near-identical chunks and enforces source diversity so one long page cannot crowd out others.
  8. Packs the highest-value chunks into a fixed token budget, adds source IDs for citation, and wraps retrieved text in delimiters so it is treated as data, not instructions.
  9. Routes by task: a small model for classification and rewriting, a stronger model for synthesis. Structured output for tool arguments. A fallback model is used on timeout or provider error.
  10. Checks that each cited ID was actually in the context, measures how well claims are supported, redacts PII, and blocks or flags low-confidence answers. A failed check produces an "I don't know" with links, never an unsupported answer.
  11. Response stream + citations + audit
Integrations
SharePointConfluenceJiraGitHub

Ingestion connectors use webhooks where available and incremental sync otherwise. Each chunk carries source, doc_id, acl_principals, updated_at and url. Live data (open tickets, PR status) is fetched through tools at query time instead of being indexed.

4 · Deep dives
RBAC
Roles map to capabilities: ask, act (write tools) and admin. Tool availability is filtered per role before the LLM sees the tool list, so the model cannot select a tool the user is not allowed to use.
JWT propagation
The user's identity flows end-to-end. Downstream calls use OAuth on-behalf-of token exchange with narrowed scopes rather than a shared service account, so each source system enforces its own authorization too.
Document permissions
ACLs are captured at ingestion and refreshed on permission-change events. Retrieval applies a pre-filter on acl_principals ∩ user_groups. A periodic job re-checks a sample of documents against the source to measure ACL drift.
PII protection
PII is detected at ingestion (tag or mask by policy) and redacted again on output. Prompts and completions in logs are redacted or hashed, with retention set per data class.
Prompt injection
Retrieved content is untrusted. It is delimited and labelled as data, tool calls are allow-listed with typed schemas, write actions need human confirmation, and an input classifier screens for known jailbreak patterns. Even a successful injection cannot exceed the user's own permissions.
Hallucination mitigation
Answers must come from the provided context. An answer with low support scores, or claims that cite IDs which were never retrieved, falls back to "insufficient evidence" with the best sources. Groundedness is tracked as a release metric.
Citation generation
Chunks get short stable IDs in the context. The model cites IDs, and code (not the model) turns IDs into titles and URLs. This keeps links real and lets the guardrail check that every citation was actually retrieved.
Observability
OpenTelemetry spans per stage (auth, retrieval, rerank, LLM, guardrail) with token counts, model, cache status and retrieved doc IDs. Quality signals (feedback, groundedness samples) sit on the same trace.
Token optimization
Fixed context budgets, chunk deduplication, conversation summarization instead of full-history replay, short system prompts with versioning, and small models for rewriting and classification steps.
Caching
Exact cache for embeddings and tool results with short TTLs. A semantic answer cache is keyed by permission scope plus query embedding, so cached answers never cross ACL boundaries. Cache entries are invalidated when a source document changes.
Latency
Streaming responses. Retrieval sources and tool calls run in parallel. Reranking is capped by candidate count. Timeouts are set per stage from a p95 budget, with graceful partial answers.
Cost controls
Per-tenant token budgets and alerts, model routing, caching, and max-iteration limits on agent loops. Cost per request is a dashboard metric next to latency and quality.
5 · Failure modes I'd call out
  • ACL drift between source and index: content leaks if sync lags. Mitigated by event-driven sync and drift audits.
  • Stale content cited as current: show updated_at and prefer fresher sources when scores tie.
  • Source outage: return a partial answer that names the unavailable source.
  • Runaway agent loop: iteration and token ceilings, then escalate.
6 · Evolution
  • v1: read-only Q&A with citations on one source, plus an evaluation harness from day one
  • v2: all four sources, hybrid retrieval and reranking, semantic cache
  • v3: write actions through MCP tools with confirmation and audit
  • v4: per-team agents, feedback-driven retrieval tuning, cost-aware routing

    08Reliability

    When AI fails

    LLM systems fail in more ways than ordinary services: slow providers, empty retrieval, confident fabrication, runaway loops. Choose a pattern to see which failures it covers.

    09Trust boundary

    Secure AI by design

    The model is not a security boundary. Identity, authorization and validation sit around it, so even a successfully manipulated model can never act beyond what the requesting user is allowed to do.

    1. USERuntrusted input
    2. AUTHENTICATIONOAuth 2.0 / OIDCshort-lived JWT
    3. AUTHORIZATIONRBACleast privilegetool scopes
    4. INPUT GUARDRAILprompt-injection screenPII maskingsize limits
    5. AGENTallow-listed toolstyped schemasmax iterations
    6. PERMISSION-AWARE RETRIEVALACL pre-filtertenant isolation
    7. LLMdelimited contextno secrets in prompts
    8. OUTPUT VALIDATIONcitation checkPII redactiondata-leakage filter
    9. AUDIT LOGwho · what · sources · toolstamper-evident
    OAuth

    Delegated access through the corporate IdP. Downstream calls use on-behalf-of exchange, never a shared super-user.

    JWT

    Validate signature, issuer, audience and expiry at the gateway. Propagate identity, not raw tokens, into logs.

    RBAC

    Roles gate both data and tools. The tool list is filtered before the model can choose.

    Least privilege

    Narrow OAuth scopes per tool. Read-only by default. Writes need explicit confirmation.

    PII masking

    Detect at ingestion, mask in prompts where possible, redact on output and in logs.

    Secret management

    Vault or a cloud secrets manager, with rotation. No keys in code, prompts, images or CI logs. Pre-commit scanning.

    Prompt injection

    Treat retrieved text and tool output as data. Allow-list tools and keep a human in the loop for side effects.

    Data leakage

    Permission-scoped caches, tenant-isolated indexes, and output filters for sensitive patterns.

    Auditability

    Every answer can be reconstructed from its trace: user, prompt version, retrieved doc IDs, tool calls and model.

    10Quality

    Evaluating AI systems

    "The answer looks good" is not an evaluation. I evaluate retrieval, generation, agent behaviour and operations separately, on versioned datasets, and run them as a regression gate in CI so prompt or model changes can't silently reduce quality.

    1. Golden setcurated Q&A + expected sources
    2. Runpipeline at a pinned version
    3. Scoremetrics + LLM-as-judge + humans
    4. Compareagainst baseline
    5. Gateblock regressions in CI
    6. Monitorsample live traffic
    AI evaluation metrics
    MetricQuestion it answersHow it's measured
    Retrieval precisionAre the retrieved chunks relevant?Labelled relevance on top-k; precision@k
    Retrieval recallDid we find the chunks that contain the answer?Expected source IDs per question; recall@k
    Context relevanceIs the packed context focused, or diluted by noise?Judge model scores each chunk against the question
    GroundednessIs every claim supported by the context?Claim extraction + entailment check against context
    FaithfulnessDoes the answer avoid contradicting or distorting sources?Judge model with rubric; spot-checked by humans
    Answer relevanceDoes it actually answer what was asked?Judge model + reference answers on the golden set
    Hallucination rateHow often are unsupported claims produced?Share of answers with ≥1 unsupported claim
    Tool accuracyRight tool, right arguments, valid schema?Expected tool calls vs actual; schema validation rate
    Agent completion rateDoes the agent finish the task within limits?Task success within max iterations and budget
    LatencyIs it fast enough for the use case?p50/p95 end-to-end and per span; time to first token
    CostIs quality affordable at scale?Tokens × price per request, per tenant, per feature
    11Interactive

    Architecture decisions

    There is rarely one right answer, only the right trade-off for the constraints. These are the defaults I start from and the conditions that would change my mind.

    12FinOps for LLMs

    AI cost engineering

    Token spend grows with usage, so cost has to be designed in from the start. Each stage below removes tokens or moves them to a cheaper model before a request reaches the expensive model.

    1. Requestwith token budget
    2. Prompt optimizationcompress, version
    3. Semantic cacheskip repeat work
    4. Model routingright-size per task
    5. Context reductionfilter, dedupe, cap
    6. LLMonly what's needed
    Token budgeting

    Explicit budgets per request, per conversation and per tenant. Over-budget requests degrade gracefully instead of failing.

    Prompt compression

    Short, versioned system prompts. Summarize conversation history instead of replaying it. Remove boilerplate instructions.

    Context filtering

    Rerank, then keep only chunks above a relevance threshold. Deduplicate near-identical passages.

    Semantic caching

    Reuse answers for paraphrased questions, scoped by permission set and invalidated on source change.

    Model routing

    Small models for classification, extraction and rewriting. Large models only for hard synthesis.

    Batching

    Batch embeddings and offline evaluation jobs. Use asynchronous batch APIs for non-interactive work.

    Smaller models

    Fine-tuned or distilled small models where evaluation shows parity on the task.

    Measure it

    Cost per request on the same dashboard as latency and quality, so trade-offs are explicit.

    Token budget estimatorIllustrative model · relative units
    Baseline100 units
    Optimized— units
    —

    Estimated relative reduction in large-model-equivalent token spend for 1,000 requests. A teaching model only: no real prices, and output tokens are held constant.

    13Case studies

    Featured projects

    Written up as engineering case studies. Where I haven't published an outcome, the card says so; I don't publish invented metrics.

    P-01

    Enterprise Agentic AI Copilot

    Agentic AI · RAG
    ProblemEnterprise questions need both unstructured knowledge (documents) and live operational data (projects, issues, metrics). The answer has to be grounded, cited and checked before anyone trusts it.
    ArchitectureSupervisor (intent + plan) → RAG agent · Tool agent · Analysis agent → Response agent → Guardrail → answer + citations + confidence; traces per run
    Tech stackPythonLangGraphLangChainFastAPIChromaDBStreamlitClaudeDockerpytest
    Key challengeKeeping answers verifiable: an LLM can cite sources it never saw or state figures that don't appear in any source.
    SolutionThe Sources section is generated by code from citation labels actually used. A guardrail checks token- and number-level support against the evidence and lowers confidence or asks for more information when support is weak. Tools are typed and exported as MCP-shaped descriptors.
    OutcomeOutcome details available during technical discussion.
    What I learnedExplicit graphs (nodes and conditional edges) make agent behaviour testable. Deterministic fallbacks, such as a demo mode without an API key, make the system reviewable by anyone. All data in the project is synthetic.
    P-02

    AI Engineering Lab (this site)

    Agents · RAG · MCP simulations
    ProblemStatic CVs don't show how someone reasons about AI architecture. Live LLM demos need keys, cost money, and fail in public.
    ArchitectureStatic site → lazy-loaded ES modules per demo → deterministic simulations (agent state machine · BM25 + hashed-vector retrieval · JSON-RPC MCP traces · seeded telemetry)
    Tech stackHTMLCSSVanilla JSGitHub ActionsGitHub Pages
    Key challengeMaking simulations technically honest without a model or backend, and making sure no demo number could be mistaken for a real statistic.
    SolutionReal algorithms where possible (BM25, cosine similarity, a token-budgeted packer, an extractive answerer that can't invent facts). Simulated values are labelled DEMO / SIMULATED. Zero runtime dependencies, and a secret scan on every deploy.
    OutcomeOutcome details available during technical discussion.
    What I learnedConstraints such as no backend and no keys force clearer explanations. If a concept can be simulated faithfully in 300 lines, it can be explained in a 5-minute conversation.
    P-03

    Image Similarity with Siamese Networks

    Deep learning · CV
    ProblemDecide whether two images show the same thing, without a classifier for every possible class.
    ArchitectureShared-weight CNN encoder (Conv2D · BatchNorm · MaxPool · Dense) on image pairs → merged embeddings → similarity head; t-SNE to inspect the learned embedding space
    Tech stackPythonKerasTensorFlowscikit-learnNumPyColab
    Key challengeBuilding balanced positive and negative pairs so the network learns similarity rather than class frequency.
    SolutionPair generation from a train/test split, a shared encoder so both inputs share one embedding space, and embedding visualization to sanity-check clustering.
    OutcomeOutcome details available during technical discussion.
    What I learnedMetric learning is the conceptual ancestor of today's embedding-based retrieval: the same "learn a space where distance means similarity" idea that powers vector search in RAG.
    P-04

    Text Detection & OCR Pipelines

    Computer vision · OCR
    ProblemExtract text from natural images, a common first step for document and image ingestion pipelines.
    ArchitectureImage upload → pretrained text detector → recognizer → word boxes + strings; compared a keras-ocr pipeline with a pretrained detection model workflow
    Tech stackPythonkeras-ocrTensorFlowMatplotlibColab
    Key challengeGetting pretrained models with conflicting framework versions to run reproducibly in a hosted notebook.
    SolutionPinned environments per notebook and the off-the-shelf detection + recognition pipeline, with results visualized as overlays for quick qualitative review.
    OutcomeOutcome details available during technical discussion.
    What I learnedReproducibility (pinned versions, explicit environments) matters as much as model choice, and the same lesson carries over to LLM systems.
